full_judgment:
7. The learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur as the last court of fact allowed the appeal and reversed the trial court's findings on the ground that the Ekrarnama was registered on 1-5-1947 and on that date there was no provision in the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 as to usufractuary mortgage, virtually it was inserted in section 95A by the President's Order No. 88 in the year 1972. 

 9. Mr khaled Mabmud Saifullah, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent-petitioners contended that as per law, the transaction was a complete usufructuary mortgage and the entire consideration for the mortgage was satisfied by usufructs of the land and in such a case limitation for filing a suit is 60 years. He also contended that the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Kalkini, Madaripur rightly decided that the suit is maintainable in its present form and not barred by limitation and the transaction in question was a complete usufructuary mortgage and thereafter passed the judgment and decree which is sustainable in law. He also submits that out of misconception of law and facts, the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur decided in appeal that Ekramama was registered on 1-5-1947 and on that date there was no provision in the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 as to usufractuary mortgage rather provision as to usufractuary mortgage was introduced in section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by the President's Order No. 88 of 1972. He adds that the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur taking the above wrong view committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, he cited the decisions passed in the cases of &m at Ali vs Abdur Rafique Mridha, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 132, Abu Bakkar vs Nazi, Ahmed, reported in 34 DL.R (AD) 237 and Khanje Ali Sikder being dead his heirs Mosammat Fatema Begum and others VS Hazi Mozaharuddin Talukder and others, reported in 8 ALR (AD) 2016(2) 26. 

 12. Before execution and registration of the sale deed No. 2351 and ekramama No. 2352 on 1-5-1947, the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 was amended by the .Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1940. By that amendment, clause (1a) of section 266 was inserted in the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 which runs as follows: 

 (a) which was so entered into before the commencement of the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1.928, 

 (b) which, being other than an usufructuary mortgage having under sub-section (1) no force or effect was so entered into after the commencement of the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1928 and before the commencement of the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1940, and was subsisting on or after the commencement of the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1940 shall be deemed to have taken effect as a complete usufructuary mortgage for the period mentioned in the instrument or for fifteen years, whichever is less." 

 13. Now, it has to be decided whether the alleged transaction was a complete usufructuary mortgage or not in the light of the above provision of Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 as amended in the year, 1940). From the recitals of the registered deed of Ekrarnama No. 2352 dated 1-5-1947 (Exhibit I), it appears that the transaction made by the plaintiff' predecessors namely Rustom Ali Karikar and Maju Bibi in favour of Arshad Ali Karikar was not an out and out sale, rather it was a conditional sale. Moreover, the contesting defendant No. I1 admitted in his additional written statement that the predecessors of the plaintiffs Rustom Ali Karikar and Maju Bibi sold out the suit property by a registered deed No. 235 I dated 1-5-1947 to Arshad Ali Karikar and on the same date Arshad Ali Karikar executed and registered a deed of Ekraniama No. 2352 with a condition that Arshad Ali Karikar would re-convey the property subject to repayment of consideration within the period of 3 years. The transaction became absolute since the mortgagors did not repay the consideration within the said three years. So, it is translucent from the recitals of the Ekrarnama (Exhibit I) and admission made in the written statement by the contesting defendant that the transaction was not an out and out sale rather it was a conditional sale. The stipulated period 3 years expired on 31-4-1950 and consideration of the transaction was already satisfied by the usufructs of the land during the said period of 3 years. There is no material on record from which it can be decided that the mortgagee or after his death his successors voluntarily restored possession of the land to the mortgagors or after their death to their successors respectively. As a result, on expiry of the said 3 years on 31-4-1950, the transaction in question became a complete usufructuary mortgage in the light of the provisions contained in Clause (la) of section 26G of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 as amended in the year, 1940). 

 14. In fact, the plaintiffs filed the suit on 9-I-2002 according to the provisions contained in Order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 190 for redemption of usufructuary mortgage. They did not file any petition under section 95 or 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 for redemption or restoration of possession of the property concerned. In such a case, limitation for filing a suit for redemption is 60 years as per provisions of Article 148 of the Limitation Act, 1908 which provides that limitation for filing a suit against a mortgage for redemption or recovery of possession of immovable property is 60 years. So, the trial court rightly decided that the transaction in question is not an out and out sale rather it was a usufructuary mortgage and the suit is not barred by limitation, since it has been filed within the period of 60 years. The trial court also decided that the suit is maintainable in its present form and there is no defect of party and accordingly decreed the suit which is sustainable in law. The decisions passed in the case of Asmat Ali vs Abdur Rafique Mridha, reported in 52 DLR (AD) 132, Abu ilakkar vs Nazir Ahmed, reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237 and Khanje Ali Sikder being dead his heirs Mosammat. Fatema Seguin and others vs Hazi Mozaharuddin Talukder and others, reported in 8 ALIT (AD) 2016 (2) 26 relating to usufractuary mortgage and limitation for filing a suit for redemption of usufractuary mortgage are relevant and very much important. In the light of those decisions, the judgment and decree passed by the trial court is justified. 

 15. But, the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur, in appeal, wrongly held that the Ekramarna was registered on 1-5-1947 and on that date there was no provision as to usufructuary mortgage in the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 to consider the transaction in question as a complete usufructuary mortgage rather provision as to usufructuary mortgage was incorporated in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 by inserting section 95A by the president's Order No. 88 in the year 1972. The learned Joint District Judge had to keep in mind that before enactment of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there was provision of usufructuary mortgage in the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 which was incorporated by inserting clause (I a) in section 260 by the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1940 and according to the provision of the said clause of section 260, the transaction in question was a complete usufructuary mortgage. 

 16. It is pertinent to mention here to remove the wrong conception of the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Madaripur that law relating to usufructuary mortgage was available in the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 and subsequently in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. According to section 95 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 maximum period for usufructuary mortgage was fifteen years which was amended by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. XXI of 1969 substituting the word "seven" for the word "fifteen" years and the section 95 was again amended by the President's Order No. 88 of 1972 with effect from 3 August, 1972 inserting section 95A. This amendment did not change the period of usufructuary mortgage nor even affect the period of limitation for filing a suit for redemption within 60 years under article 148 of the Limitation Act, 1908 and to file a suit under order 34 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. In fact, objective of insertion of section 95A in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 are as follows:
